posts.title: HM-630 second generation: what changed in the spindle
posts.excerpt: The second-generation HM-630 keeps its bed, its pallet changer and its price class. The change is inside the spindle cartridge, and it is measured in microns.
posts.content:
The second generation of the HM-630 keeps the bed, the column and the 630 mm pallet changer of the first. What changed is the spindle cartridge, which Mika Oda's team redesigned over eighteen months and which now ships in every machine built from this autumn.

The first change is the bearing preload. The earlier cartridge used a fixed preload set at assembly. The new one uses a hydraulic preload that is lower at 14,000 rpm and higher at low speed, so a roughing cut in cast iron and a finishing cut in aluminium both run on the bearing setting they actually need.

The second change is cooling. Coolant now circulates through the spindle housing and the front bearing seat on a separate loop, held to within 0.3 degrees of the machine bed. In the inspection room at 20 degrees, thermal growth at the spindle nose after eight hours of continuous cutting fell from 14 microns to 5 microns.

The third change is smaller but customers notice it first: the drawbar. The new drawbar holds the tool with 18 kilonewtons instead of 14, which removes the faint chatter we saw in deep face milling with long tools. Tool life on a 125 mm face mill rose by about a fifth in our own cutting trials.

We tested the new cartridge for 2,000 hours on a demonstration machine before releasing it. It cut transmission housings in grey iron for three shifts a day, and the ball-bar trace at the end was inside 3 microns, the same as on the first day.

Existing HM-630 owners can fit the new cartridge. It is a drop-in exchange: Tomas Lindqvist's service team removes the old cartridge, fits the new one and re-runs the 72-hour test on site. The work takes four days, and we hold the price steady for the first twelve months.

If you would like the test data for the new spindle, including the thermal curves, write to the sales office and ask for the HM-630 technical note. We will send the numbers, not a brochure.

posts.title: Why our castings rest for a year before machining
posts.excerpt: Every bed and column we build sits outdoors for twelve months before it is machined. It looks slow. It is the cheapest accuracy we know.
posts.content:
Every bed, column and saddle we build arrives from the foundry as a rough grey iron casting, and then it waits. It rests on timber in the yard at Riverside Works for twelve months, through a winter, a spring and a summer, before a cutter touches it.

The reason is internal stress. When iron cools in a mould, the thick sections cool slower than the thin ones, and the casting locks that difference in as stress. Machined straight away, the stress is released unevenly and the part moves. A bed that was flat to 5 microns on Friday can be 20 microns out on Monday.

Weather does the work for us. Frost and summer heat cycle the casting by thirty degrees or more, and each cycle lets a little stress relax. We measure a sample of castings every three months with a laser and a dial gauge. After about nine months, movement falls below 2 microns a year, and that is the number we wait for.

After twelve months the casting is rough machined and then rests again for two weeks, because even a cutter relieves some stress. Only then do we finish the guideways and send the bed to the scraping bay. We scrape to 3 microns over 1.2 metres, and the bed holds that figure because it has already finished moving.

We have tried faster routes. Thermal stress relief in a furnace works, and for small parts we use it. For beds over three tonnes, we found that furnace relief left a casting that still drifted by 6 to 8 microns in its first year of service. Waiting costs us warehouse space and interest. A customer's scrap parts cost more.

The yard now holds about 320 tonnes of iron, enough for roughly two years of production. It is not an efficient use of money, and Ren Hagane has been asked about it by every accountant who has visited. His answer is always the same: ask the customer whose machine is twenty-five years old and still in tolerance.

posts.title: Visiting us at the autumn machine-tool fair in Hall 4
posts.excerpt: Find us in Hall 4, stand 4120, from 6 to 10 October. We bring a running HM-630 and the engineers who built it.
posts.content:
Hagane Machinery will exhibit at the autumn machine-tool fair from 6 to 10 October. You will find us in Hall 4, stand 4120, next to the main aisle and opposite the grinding area.

On the stand we are bringing a running HM-630 horizontal machining centre, cutting a gearbox housing in grey iron every day at 10.00, 13.00 and 16.00. The cycle takes 38 minutes. We will measure the finished housing on a coordinate measuring machine beside the stand and hand the printed report to anyone who asks.

Alongside the machine, a smaller area shows a cut-away HV spindle cartridge and a section of a scraped guideway, with the blue dye marks still visible. Aiko Mori will be on the stand on Tuesday and Thursday to show how a surface plate finds a high spot of 2 microns, and to let visitors try the scraper.

Mika Oda and Tomas Lindqvist will be there for the whole week. Mika will answer questions on spindles and thermal behaviour, and Tomas will talk about service, spare parts and retrofit of older HM machines. If you operate an HM-500 or an HM-300, bring the serial number and we will tell you what can be done.

If you would like a meeting at a fixed time, write to the sales office before 30 September and we will reserve half an hour with the right engineer. We would rather talk to you about your part than about our machine, so please bring a drawing, a sample or a photograph.

Visitors from our customers' plants are welcome at a quiet corner of the stand, where coffee and a table are kept free all week. We look forward to seeing you in Hall 4.

posts.title: A new service base in Monterrey
posts.excerpt: Our sixth service base opens in Monterrey on 1 October, with a spindle exchange, a parts store and four engineers.
posts.content:
On 1 October Hagane Machinery opens its sixth service base, in Monterrey, Mexico. It joins Ostmere, Gothenburg, Stuttgart, Lyon and Taichung, and it is the first of our bases in the Americas.

The reason is simple. Over the last five years the number of Hagane machines in northern Mexico has grown from 90 to more than 310, mostly HM-630 machines in automotive plants. Until now, a spare spindle came by air from Ostmere, and the quickest delivery took two days. From October, it takes four hours.

The base occupies 1,800 square metres in an industrial estate near the airport. It holds a parts store with about 2,400 line items, a spindle exchange with eight cartridges for the HM and HV series, and a small workshop with a surface plate and a laser interferometer.

Four engineers will work there from the start. Two came from the Ostmere service department and have each spent more than ten years on the road; two were hired locally from machine-tool maintenance teams. All four have completed the full Hagane training in Ostmere, including a week at the scraping bench.

The base will answer the service hotline from 07.00 to 17.00 local time, with the evening hours covered by the European base. Customers in Mexico will have the response times already stated in their service agreements: a first reply within the hour, remote diagnosis within four hours and an engineer on site within 24 hours.

Tomas Lindqvist travelled to Monterrey in August to set up the store. He says that the most useful thing in the building is a plain wall board, listing for every customer the serial numbers, the spindle type and the last service date. Please write to the service desk if you want your machine added.

posts.title: Hand scraping, explained by Aiko Mori
posts.excerpt: Aiko Mori has scraped machine beds for thirty-one years. She explains blue dye, surface plates and why a machine made this way holds its accuracy.
posts.content:
Aiko Mori leads the scraping and assembly bay at Riverside Works. She has worked at the same bench for thirty-one years, and she says that nobody understands scraping until they have scraped something for a week.

The idea is simple. A machined guideway looks flat, but under magnification it is a field of tiny hills and valleys, each a few microns high. Scraping removes the highest hills by hand, until the surface carries weight evenly. It is the only way we know to make two surfaces that fit each other, instead of two surfaces that are each flat.

The process uses a surface plate, a tin of blue dye and a hand scraper with a carbide blade. Aiko spreads a thin layer of dye on the plate, lays the guideway over it and slides it once. The high spots pick up blue. She scrapes only the blue spots, a few strokes each, and then repeats.

A guideway is finished when it shows at least twenty contact points in every 25 millimetre square, spread evenly across the whole length. The target is flatness of 3 microns over 1.2 metres. An HM-630 bed takes three people about six weeks to scrape, and nobody is allowed to hurry.

Why do we still do it? Because scraped surfaces hold oil. The small valleys left between the contact points work as little reservoirs, and the sliding axis floats on a thin film instead of grinding against dry metal. Machines scraped this way keep their accuracy for decades, as we see on HM-300 machines from 1988 that still cut in tolerance.

Aiko says that after thirty-one years she can feel a high spot of 2 microns with her thumb. She trains every apprentice to find it by touch first, then to confirm it with the dye. It takes about a year before a new person's work passes without correction.

If you visit Riverside Works, ask to see the scraping bay. You will see blue hands, a surface plate and a long quiet, and you will understand why our machines take seven to nine months to build.

posts.title: Retrofitting a 1994 HM-500 for another twenty years
posts.excerpt: A pump manufacturer asked whether its 1994 HM-500 was worth keeping. After a retrofit it holds 4 microns again, at about a third of the price of a new machine.
posts.content:
In March a pump manufacturer in Gothenburg asked Tomas Lindqvist's team a plain question: is our 1994 HM-500 worth keeping? The machine had cut pump housings for thirty years, but positioning had drifted to 25 microns and the control was no longer supported.

Our engineers measured the machine on site with a laser and a ball-bar. The news was good. The bed and the column, scraped in 1994, were still flat to within 6 microns. The guideways showed light wear in the middle third of the travel, but no scoring. The weak parts were the spindle, the ball screws and the electronics.

We proposed a retrofit in four parts: a new spindle cartridge of the current type, new ball screws with pre-tensioned nuts on all three axes, a modern control with new drives, and a local re-scraping of the worn middle section of the Y axis guideway. Aiko Mori's team did the scraping on site over five days.

The work took nine weeks, of which the machine was out of service for seven. The customer kept a second machine running during that time. The retrofit price was about a third of the price of a new HM-630, and the customer kept its fixtures, its tooling and its programs, which saved another month of qualification.

After the retrofit, we ran the 72-hour test on site. The ball-bar trace closed inside 4 microns, and the positioning error over the full travel was 6 microns, better than the original specification of 10 microns. Spindle growth after four hours of cutting measured 7 microns.

We now offer a fixed list of retrofit packages for the HM-300, HM-500 and HM-630 series, with prices stated before the survey. A survey takes two days and costs nothing if you order the retrofit. If it is not worth the money, we will tell you so in writing.

The HM-500 in Gothenburg is back in production on two shifts. The customer expects it to run another twenty years, and we hope to be asked about it again in 2046.
